headlines.summary: As crypto evolves past its trading roots, and global markets shift to 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure.
headlines.article_text: Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the use of Ripple's digital dollar, RLUSD, broadening trading and financing options for institutional clients and improving Robinhood's internal money management. The partnership meets Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing more of its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients. As the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets shift to 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure. In this article HOOD Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Ripple and Robinhood Getty Images Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD , strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management. The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year . It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients. "Utility is what moves stablecoins forward. Working with Ripple, Bitstamp and Robinhood will have access to RLUSD for institutional settlement, Ripple Treasury for our operations and Ripple Prime for financing," Robinhood Crypto General Manager Johann Kerbrat said in a statement shared with CNBC. "That is what a connected, global financial system looks like." Workhorse Stablecoins have long been a workhorse of the crypto world, giving traders a way to move money among exchanges, buy and sell crypto assets, and park funds between trades without having to convert back into traditional currency. But as the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets move toward 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure because of their ability to enable near-instant settlement and move dollar-denominated value at any time, regardless of traditional banking hours. As firms look to do more with stablecoins beyond simply listing them on exchanges, stablecoin issuers are betting they'll favor a one-stop-shop approach that bundles the technology and services needed to move money, settle trades and manage cash. "Stablecoins have evolved from a crypto trading tool into a critical piece of financial infrastructure," Ripple President Monica Long told CNBC. "The clearest evidence of this is where they're now being embedded — from corporate payments to capital markets. Our partnership with Robinhood reflects that evolution." "This is about much more than trading," she added. "It's about fundamentally changing how money moves and is managed — giving institutions the ability to operate 24/7/365, unlocking liquidity and putting capital to work more efficiently." Circle Internet Group, a Ripple competitor, is positioning itself for a similar future, where winning platforms, in addition to issuing stablecoins, also provide the infrastructure to put them to work. Earlier this year, for example, it launched the Circle Payments Network, connecting financial institutions and payment providers using its flagship USDC stablecoin and other digital assets for cross-border payments. The network is Circle's answer to the 8-year-old Ripple Payments business, a service that helps businesses move money across borders, using any of several assets moving through that system, including USDC, Ripple-created XRP and, as of its debut in December 2024, RLUSD. RLUSD's market cap has grown to more than $2.5 billion . Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC still dominate the total stablecoin market, which now exceeds $300 billion . RLUSD will also be listed on Robinhood's trading platform, and is currently available to traders on Bitstamp as well as Robinhood Chain, the company's home-grown blockchain for tokenized stocks and other assets. Robinhood, which reports third-quarter results for the three months ended in September after the market closes, rose about 2.5% in early trading Tuesday, snapping a three-day decline. headlines.title: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps and expands cloud chip lineup
headlines.summary: Oracle is integrating OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Codex into its applications and plans to add Google TPUs and OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip to OCI.
headlines.article_text: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps, expands cloud chip lineup Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Oracle is adding OpenAI's ChatGPT and Codex to its application stack, extending enterprise access to OpenAI tools. Oracle said OCI will add Google TPUs, OpenAI's Jalapeño chip and Cerebras hardware as customers seek more silicon options. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk for a keynote at Oracle AI World. In this article OPENAI.FG CBRS ORCL GOOGL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Oracle on Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration with OpenAI that brings the artificial intelligence lab's ChatGPT and Codex into the software maker's applications to make databases more actionable. Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle's president of Cloud Infrastructure, told CNBC at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas that using ChatGPT "allows anybody to build an application, deploy it, manage it." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk on stage for an Oracle AI World keynote on Tuesday at 12:40 p.m. ET. For OpenAI, the announcement represents another example of the frontier lab's push into the enterprise market, just one day after its key competitor, Anthropic , filed its S-1 as it heads toward an initial public offering . Oracle's database plays a crucial role in underpinning businesses across healthcare and finance in logging and securing data. Thiagarajan said his team observed OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model get trained at Oracle's Stargate data center campus in Abilene, Texas, and could see the real-time benefits. "More businesses are choosing OpenAI as we make it easier to put AI to work through the tools and systems they already use," said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, in the press release. Oracle also said Tuesday that it is making different hardware accessible on its cloud infrastructure, including Google 's tensor processing unit AI chips and OpenAI's Jalapeño chip. "Now customers can actually have infinite possibilities in terms of how they can drive AI," Thiagarajan said. It is the first time Google's custom chips will run on another hyperscaler's cloud, and illustrates how the companies are increasingly looking for opportunities to get their hardware in the hands of the frontier labs. When asked whether this marks a pivot away from Nvidia GPUs, Thiagarajan said no, adding that Nvidia chips are "the best, most fungible," and that the AI market remains incredibly large. OpenAI's Jalapeno chip and Cerebras will also run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The Cerebras deal is material, but the AI chipmaker won't be disclosing the scale because it's in a quiet period, a Cerebras spokesperson said. Cerebras stock climbed about 8% following the news. Oracle shares were up nearly 5% on Tuesday. The announcement comes seven months after market-leading cloud Amazon Web Services announced plans to bring Cerebras hardware into its data centers , a major point of validation. Thiagarajan also addressed Oracle's multibillion New Mexico data center dubbed Project Jupiter and the ongoing pushback it's receiving from the local community. He said Jupiter represents just one of the 30-40 different data center projects in development, per quarter, for the company. "We're actually not too worried about what we're doing because I think we're building global infrastructure," he said. A hearing to address air quality permitting is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Sunland Park, where the controversial data center has already broken ground. The political pushback tied to the project prompted Oracle to deliver a force majeure notice to its backer Blue Owl Capital last month. Right now, Oracle maintains that the project is on schedule. Investors are now counting down to Oracle's investor day, where investors will want to see if the company can back its fiscal year 2030 revenue targets and if the margin profile of its cloud deals has changed due to the rising cost of capital. Bank of America analysts wrote to clients that updates on Oracle's major data center projects are among the topics they expect clarity on at the meeting. Oracle shares are down more than 30% this year due in part to concerns about how the company plans to finance its ambitious digital infrastructure pipeline. —CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed to this article Oracle stock chart. headlines.summary: Follow CNBC's 2026 Workforce Executive Summit for live updates on Walmart's AI strategy, changing job skills, hiring, employee benefits and the future of work.
headlines.article_text: CNBC Workforce Executive Summit 2026 live updates: AI at work Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Mikkelwilliam | E+ | Getty Images Today's workplace faces a litany of challenges. Whether it's shifting power dynamics between employers and employees, the accelerating impact of artificial intelligence on how we work and the skills we need, or the financial stresses that employees of all ranks are feeling, these issues and more are challenging the cohesion of workplace communities. To address these issues, CNBC is convening its premiere council of human resource executives in New York City on Tuesday for the annual CNBC Workforce Executive Summit. The event is exclusive to members of CNBC's Workforce Executive Council. For more about the WEC and to apply for membership, visit www.cnbccouncils.com/wec . 8 Min Ago Health insurance costs are growing, with no end in sight watch now VIDEO 10:03 10:03 Rising costs of health benefits: Total cost per employee expected to rise 8.2% in 2027 Squawk Box Most Americans under age 65 — about 166 million people — get health insurance via employer-sponsored health plans. That is generally subsided by their employers, who cover a large portion of the monthly premium payments workers pay. The average worker paid $6,850 of annual premiums in 2025, while employers contributed more than $20,000 per worker, according to KFF. In 2027, the cost for employers to provide health benefits will rise by an estimated 8.2% per worker, on average. That represents the largest increase since 2003, even with additional cost-reduction measures by employers, according to Marsh. Aon, another consulting firm, expects employer costs to jump 9.5% in 2027 — the fourth consecutive year of "elevated" healthcare costs, "extending one of the most sustained periods of health care inflation employers have faced in decades," the firm said in a press release in August. Growth in the cost of deductibles and family premiums has each outpaced inflation over the past decade , rising 54% and 53%, respectively, versus an overall inflation rate of 36%, according to KFF. All of those cost increases are likely leading to cuts in benefits next year for workers who are covered by plans from their jobs: Nearly 6 out of 10 employers — 59% — plan to make cost-cutting changes to health benefits in 2027, including by adding higher deductibles, according to Marsh. It polled more than 1,800 employers from June 10 to August 10. HealthEquity CFO James Lucania will be speaking later today at the CNBC Workforce Summit about how CHROs and benefits managers can use AI to streamline healthcare costs, and at the same time, make out-of-pocket payments easier for employees to understand and manage, all while helping each of them get the care they need. 23 Min Ago AI is fueling uncertainty in the job market A sign on the Microsoft campus in Redmond, Washington, US, Oct. 26, 2026. David Ryder | Reuters There are many forces changing the workplace. But few are having the impact that AI is, shifting roles and job expectations, as well as headcount. Microsoft announced this week that it is offering voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees, a measure that comes as the company strives to balance a costly AI build-out with efficiency. The software company has been ramping up its spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand as it supplies cloud services to a number of AI companies. The offer follows a voluntary retirement program announced at Microsoft this past spring and 4,800 jobs cut in July. American Express said last week that it would be cutting thousands of employees as the leading credit card company prepares for artificial intelligence to take over more of its internal processes. Amex is eliminating 5% of its global workforce and taking a $336 million restructuring charge, CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts Friday on the company's third-quarter earnings call. The firm had almost 77,000 employees at the end of 2025. Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC in an interview that the restructuring was to make American Express "leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI." "You don't want to automate processes that are not optimally structured," Le Caillec said. "So what we're doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years." The Amex announcement reflects a broader trend across financial services, where banks are working to replace repetitive roles with AI automation. On Thursday, Barclays confirmed plans to trim 5,000 jobs — also roughly 5% of its staff — in another tech-driven cost initiative. The moves come even as the sector is enjoying robust profits from growing consumer spending and resilient credit. Skydance also announced voluntary buyouts following its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, a step driven largely by the consolidation, but it also comes as executives acknowledge that AI will transform the company. In addition, Qualcomm cut jobs earlier this month as the company pivots towards AI data centers and non-smartphone markets. - Colleen McKown 38 Min Ago What role do cities play in AI oversight? watch now VIDEO 4:51 04:51 NYC council speaker: Need for regulation was big takeaway from NYC AI hearing The Exchange Earlier this month, the New York City Council held a legislative investigation concerning artificial intelligence safety risks, with senior leaders from Anthropic , OpenAI, Google and Meta testifying under oath about the potential dangers of the technology and outlined current safety measures. The hearing took place amid the intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models. It also came as the questions over who is responsible for keeping the technology in-check also grow. With concerns over the federal government's oversight of AI abound, cities are stepping up. New York City Council speaker Julie Menin opened that hearing by singling out the federal government's light-touch approach to AI after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary accord with tech leaders in Washington last week. "The idea that artificial intelligence is going to self-regulate defies all reason," she said at the hearing. Menin, who is appearing at today's Workforce Executive Summit, told CNBC's Kelly Evans on "The Exchange" following the hearing that one of the biggest takeaways was that the AI labs "really weren't able to answer some of the most rudimentary questions, such as what is the risk of a cataclysmic event happening? What do they feel the risk is? Will they agree, for example, not to release any new model that hasn't passed an internal or third-party validator safety check?" "I think what really came out of the hearing is the need for regulation," Menin told Evans. "We have to remember that the pharmaceutical industry doesn't self-regulate; they have the FDA. The airline industry doesn't self-regulate; they have the FAA, and similarly, we need to ensure that with artificial intelligence, we have smart safeguard rails in place." Menin told Evans that much of the responsibility when it comes to legislating AI will fall to localities, and she hopes that some of the legislation New York City is putting into effect will serve as a blueprint for other jurisdictions. "We certainly hope the federal government will opt to regulate," she said, adding that she sees one of the most important regulations as the issue of third-party regulation. "You cannot have these companies self-select a validator," she said. Menin added that she does not want to stifle innovation, but cautions that "with innovation, really comes responsibility, and I think it actually instills faith and confidence in the products that these companies are releasing, the new models that they're releasing, if we have smart and sensible safeguards in place." - Colleen McKown

Bruce Bennett | Getty Images JetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but shares surged as the carrier's upbeat forecast that it will return to profitability appeared to calm investors after a Monday rout. JetBlue stock was up nearly 19% in early trading Tuesday after hitting a new low a day earlier as investors fretted about the company's financial future. The Monday drop came after the Wall Street Journal reported Friday that a group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners . "I think there is a significant disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results are demonstrating, CEO Joanna Geraghty said on the company's earnings call Tuesday. The airline said its revenue per available seat mile, a key metric measuring how much operating revenue a carrier generates for every seat flown one mile, would be up as much as 22% in the fourth quarter, bringing the annual increase to an expected 13.5% to 14.5% Read more about airlines' race to win over big spenders Alaska Airlines unveils massive premium cabin overhaul in high-end travel race Budget airline king Bill Franke warms to first-class seats and premium upgrades United ditches more economy seats to make room for bigger premium cabins with new layouts Caviar and privacy: Airlines' business-class wars are here American Airlines is arriving late to the luxury travel boom. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million. The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines. JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday. "Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow." Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG: Loss per share: 60 cents adjusted vs. a loss of 55 cents expected Revenue: $2.81 billion vs. $2.82 billion expected JetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares . JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period. The airline has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals. It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines , which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines . CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month. Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected becuase of the wings production pace. Boeing stock was down about 9% during the call. "I know everybody wants us to go faster but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday. Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday. "Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality." Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it. Third-quarter earnings The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit. For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program. Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025. The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion. Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier. Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said. Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do." Certification wins The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet. And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10 , the largest in the Max family. headlines.article_text: Coca-Cola (KO) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Coca-Cola topped Wall Street's estimates for its quarterly earnings and revenue. The company hiked its full-year forecast for the third straight quarter. In this article KO Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Multipacks of Coca-Cola Original Taste glass bottles, 4x200ml, line a supermarket shelf in Bari, Italy, on September 15, 2026. Matteo Della Torre | Nurphoto | Getty Images Coca-Cola on Tuesday raised its full-year outlook for the third straight quarter, despite lackluster demand in its home market. For the full year, Coke now expects comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from its prior forecast of an increase in the range of 9% to 10%. The beverage giant also anticipates that its organic revenue will climb at least 5%, a slight increase from its previous outlook of approximately 5% growth. CEO Henrique Braun attributed the company's strong results to its "speed and discipline" despite the "uneven environment," he said on the company's earnings conference call. Looking ahead to 2027, the company expects consumer behavior to remain unchanged, CFO John Murphy said. In recent quarters, Braun and other executives have said North American shoppers are under pressure, stretched thin by inflation and economic uncertainty, and looking for value. But the beverage giant has also said consumers are still buying its drinks, from premium brands like Fairlife to its namesake soda. Shares of the company fell less than 1% in morning trading on its gloomy forecast for the consumer environment. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street analysts surveyed by LSEG were expecting: Earnings per share: 91 cents adjusted vs. 88 cents expected Revenue: $13.4 billion vs. $12.92 billion expected Coke reported fiscal third-quarter net income attributable to shareholders of $4.01 billion, or 93 cents per share, up from $3.7 billion, or 86 cents per share, a year earlier. Excluding transaction gains and other items, Coke earned 91 cents per share. Net sales rose 7% to $13.4 billion. Coke's organic revenue, which strips out acquisitions, divestitures and foreign currency, also climbed 7% in the quarter. For the second straight quarter, the company's unit case volume increased 5%, helped by higher demand outside of North America. Coke's home market reported flat volume. However, the company's North American business would have reported volume growth if not for the timing of the Fourth of July holiday and the monthslong shortage of Topo Chico, a sparkling water brand Coke owns, Murphy told CNBC. "The underlying momentum remains quite strong," he said. "Consumer sentiment is largely unchanged in the sense that, wherever you are on the income scale, you're looking for value, and I think our system here has done a good job interpreting that." In North America, Coke's at-home business is faring better than its away-from-home segment, which includes restaurants, movie theaters and amusement parks. The restaurant industry is still under pressure, and Coke expects that to continue through the rest of the year, Murphy told analysts on the company's earnings conference call. Globally, Coke's sparkling soft drinks business saw volume increase 5% during the quarter, lifted by growth of Coke, Coke Zero Sugar and Diet Coke. Diet Coke is having a "resurgence," Murphy told CNBC. Gen Z consumers in the U.S. have nicknamed it a "fridge cigarette," while consumers in India threw Diet Coke parties as shortages tied to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran have made the drink scarce. "It's a brand that's almost reinventing itself with the next generation of consumers," he said. Coke has also gained market share as rival PepsiCo sees its soda business struggle, according to Murphy. Still, some of Coke's soda brands, like Sprite, have "some work to do." Coke's water, sports, coffee and tea division also saw volume climb by 5%. Increased demand for its water, which includes its premium Smartwater brand, fueled the growth. Demand for its tea and coffee was flat, while sports drinks declined. The company's juice, value-added dairy and plant-based beverages business reported flat volume, despite growth in brands like Fairlife and Minute Maid.
